energy_regime.quote: at the record collision energy of 13.6 trillion electronvolts (TeV) - 6.8 TeV per beam
energy_regime.value: Proton-proton collisions at 7-13.6 TeV centre-of-mass energy; lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair

facility_roles.note: CERN hosts ATLAS at LHC Point 1 on its Meyrin site.
facility_roles.quote: ATLAS is a general-purpose particle physics experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN.

intervals.label: Letter of Intent
intervals.note: INSPIRE's experiment record CERN-LHC-ATLAS gives the same date in date_proposed (1992-10-01). End = submission of the Technical Proposal.
intervals.quote: Submitted on 1 October 1992 (being considered the birthdate of the collaboration), the Letter of Intent was a 108-page document which made the physics case for a general purpose proton-proton experiment at the LHC.

intervals.label: Technical Proposal
intervals.note: CERN-LHCC-94-43 / LHCC-P-2. End = the approval date in the INSPIRE experiment record.
intervals.quote: a Technical Proposal (TP) was developed and submitted in December 1994.

intervals.label: approval
intervals.note: date_approved = 1996-01-31 in the INSPIRE experiment record; ATLAS's own account dates formal construction approval by CERN's Director-General to July 1997, which is the end of this interval.

intervals.label: construction and installation
intervals.note: End set at the September 2008 first beam; the JINST detector paper (August 2008) describes the detector 'as the installation of the ATLAS detector is nearing completion'.
intervals.quote: In July 1997, formal construction approval for ATLAS was given by CERN's Director General, starting with the calorimeters.

intervals.label: commissioning and first collisions
intervals.note: First proton-proton collisions recorded in ATLAS on 23 November 2009 at 0.9 TeV (src:atlas-first-collisions-news; INSPIRE date_started 2009-11-23). Ends the day before the first 7 TeV collisions.
intervals.quote: The final product, weighing about 7,000 tonnes and 45 by 25 meters in size, saw its first beam on 10 September 2008.

end.note: Run 1 ended in early 2013 with Long Shutdown 1; no CERN or ATLAS page fetched in this session gives the exact date, so year precision only.

intervals.label: Run 1
intervals.note: Start = the first 7 TeV collisions on 30 March 2010 (home.cern key figures: 'first high-energy collisions (7 TeV) on 30 March 2010').
intervals.quote: The first attempt for collisions at 7 TeV (3.5 TeV per beam) is scheduled for 30 March.

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 1
intervals.note: Bounded by the sourced facts that Run 1 ended in early 2013 and that the LHC's second run covered 2015-2018.

intervals.label: Run 2
intervals.note: End from 'On 3 December, the LHC's second run came to an end after three fantastic years' (src:cern-run2-conclusion-2018).
intervals.quote: During this second run (2015-2018), the LHC performed beyond expectations

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 2 / Phase-I upgrade
intervals.note: Start = the 3 December 2018 dateline of CERN's LS2 announcement; end = first Run 3 physics collisions.
intervals.quote: The return of LHC beams comes after more than three years of upgrade and maintenance work, with new detector systems and electronic infrastructure installed 100 metres underground in the ATLAS cavern.

intervals.label: Run 3
intervals.note: End at month precision: CERN switched the LHC off for LS3 and announced it on 29 June 2026.
intervals.quote: At 16.47 CEST, the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) officially kicked off its third period of operation (Run 3).

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 3 / Phase-II upgrade
intervals.note: Replacement of the inner tracker by the ITk, installation of the HGTD, new trigger/DAQ and new calorimeter and muon front-end electronics.
intervals.quote: They will all be installed and commissioned during LS3 in time for the start of Run 4, currently planned for 2029.

intervals.label: Run 4 (HL-LHC)
intervals.note: Schedule value. CONFLICT: CERN's accelerator pages date the start of HL-LHC operation to 2030 (see accelerator:hl-lhc).
intervals.quote: The high-luminosity phase of the LHC (HL-LHC) will provide an order of magnitude more data starting from 2029.

quantity.quote: at the record collision energy of 13.6 trillion electronvolts (TeV) - 6.8 TeV per beam
ATLAS has the dimensions of a cylinder, 46m long, 25m in diameter, and sits in a cavern 100m below ground.
The ATLAS detector weighs 7,000 tonnes, similar to the weight of the Eiffel Tower.
The inner detector is immersed in a 2 T solenoidal field.
It sits in a cavern 100 m below ground near the main CERN site, close to the village of Meyrin in Switzerland.

name: ATLAS
notes: The 2008 JINST detector paper gives the detector length as 44 m; atlas.cern and home.cern give 46 m. Both are recorded (see detector:atlas).
ATLAS was formed from the merger of the ASCOT and EAGLE proposals; no page fetched in this session states that on the record, so it is not carried as a sourced value.

physics_goals.locator: atlas.cern, Physics, 'Higgs Boson and Electroweak Physics'
physics_goals.value: Study the Higgs boson and the Brout-Englert-Higgs field

physics_goals.quote: ATLAS studies these particles and searches for others to determine if the particles we know are indeed elementary
physics_goals.value: Test the Standard Model and determine whether the known particles are elementary

physics_goals.quote: The hermetic construction of ATLAS, however, makes it possible to search for this 'dark matter'
By searching for imbalances in the production of matter and antimatter, we seek to understand why our universe appears to comprise only matter
physics_goals.value: Understand the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe

physics_goals.quote: To explain the difference we look for such exotic phenomena as extra dimensions, gravitons, and microscopic black holes
physics_goals.value: Search for extra dimensions, gravitons and microscopic black holes

physics_goals.quote: Proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions...recreate the conditions immediately following the Big Bang
physics_goals.value: Recreate and study the conditions immediately following the Big Bang in proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions

summary.plain: ATLAS is one of the two big general-purpose experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Its 7000-tonne detector sits in a cavern 100 metres underground and records what comes out of proton collisions. In 2012 ATLAS and CMS announced the discovery of the Higgs boson.
summary.technical: General-purpose pp and heavy-ion collider experiment at LHC Point 1. Proposed by Letter of Intent in October 1992, approved in January 1996, first collisions November 2009; Runs 1-3 at 7-13.6 TeV. Physics programme spans Higgs, electroweak, top, QCD, heavy ions and searches beyond the Standard Model.

unique_capabilities.quote: The muon spectrometer defines the overall dimensions of the ATLAS detector.
unique_capabilities.value: The only LHC detector using a large air-core toroid magnet system for muon measurement, which sets its overall size

unique_capabilities.quote: The LAr forward calorimeters provide both electromagnetic and hadronic energy measurements, and extend the pseudorapidity coverage to |eta| = 4.9.
unique_capabilities.value: Hermetic 4-pi coverage out to |eta| = 4.9 in calorimetry, enabling missing-transverse-energy searches
